body.x: Advances in networking technology have given us innovative mobile communications devices like the smartphone, while the development of multimedia technology has brought us high-definition TVs and other high-quality video devices. But this is from the perspective of those who only consume media, not those who make it. Media content creators, and in particular broadcasting companies, need hardware and software that combine network and multimedia technology that is several steps beyond what is experienced by the average person. Indeed, we can say that broadcasting equipment is at the vanguard of IT technology.

It is interesting to follow the movements of the companies that are supplying cutting-edge broadcasting equipment. They are pouring considerable energy into the development of solutions that are optimized for high-definition broadcasting and interactive broadcasting, both of which have been rising in prominence recently. Little could be more fascinating than comparing the skill of large, established companies with impressive backgrounds and the eye-popping ideas of up-and-coming firms able to respond deftly to a rapidly changing market.

The 2012 Korea Electronics Show gives you an opportunity to get a glimpse of the current position of such broadcasting equipment companies. Of particular interest is equipment used to build a network environment for broadcasts that can cover a wide area. One example is the U-SOTEC system produced by Karak Electronics, a main controller for managing a broadcasting network system that offers a variety of functions including multi-source broadcasting, mixing, and TTS. This controller not only upgrades performance and functionality but also is more convenient to operate. In addition, Dwel’s Uni-A/V switcher is able to convert a variety of full HD broadcasting sources, all in one place. The fact that it can be controlled remotely from a PC connected to a LAN only increases its utility.

The show also offers plenty of solutions for increasing the efficiency and convenience of producing media content yourself at the broadcasting studio. Kirin Industrial is offering high-quality LED lighting equipment which adds to the energy and realism on stage. This product represents a distinct improvement over previous lighting equipment in terms of brightness, service life, and energy consumption. Beyond this, Bon Electronics is exhibiting a field monitor that can handle monitoring and editing work outside while still maintaining a bright, clear full-HD image quality. Another product the company is featuring is a wireless transmitter and receiver that can reliably send broadcasting data for editing with no cable required.

In addition to these options, there are also quite a few products that offer a big change in form while maintaining the same basic functions of products on the shelf today. One good example is Postium Korea, which is showcasing a rack-shaped dual monitor and triple monitor that will come in handy for anyone who needs to monitor and edit information from multiple broadcasts at the same time.

Naturally, this shouldn’t be taken to mean that only professionals working in the studio can take advantage of the products on display. Indeed, there are a variety of items here that will demonstrate the fact that, as a rule, technology that is developed for professionals can eventually be put to good use in products for ordinary consumers. Take the antenna for receiving terrestrial digital broadcasts that was developed by Spectrum. The antennas developed by this company feature such stunning reception and convenience that they can be installed inside a building without interfering with performance. Then there is Radsone, which is showing off DNS (digital noise suppression) that can be applied to virtually all audio equipment, including CD players, amps, cell phones, car stereos, and smartphones. Implement this technology, and you can eliminate unnecessary interference while simultaneously enjoying crystal-clear sound that is very close to the original.

So what is the common thread running through all of the latest broadcasting equipment being released at this year’s show? It is not merely stats and specs that have been improved in the products you see here: rather, their convenience has been enhanced and they have been upgraded with supplemental features. Particularly interesting is the fact that ideas that had generally been used in smartphones, PCs, TVs, and wired and wireless routers could be so easily applied – with some tweaking – in the development of broadcasting equipment intended for use by professionals.

In the past, professional-quality equipment had high performance value but was inconvenient to use. In contrast, products for the general consumer scored high marks in convenience but left a lot to be desired in terms of performance. It’s also true that, for far too long, people just took this for granted. It appears, however, that this may no longer apply. We are starting to see a new attitude - that we should not be tied to yesterday’s assumptions and should be willing to accept and apply any advantageous trait no matter where we may find it. This is the reason why we should be paying attention to the Broadcasting Equipment Hall at KES 2012.
